title: Know What You Carry: Principle 3 of The Way Through
author: Asha Wright
summary: Wright reflects on moving from Melbourne to Brisbane nearly thirty years ago, using the experience to illustrate Principle 3 of her framework 'The Way Through': that a change in location or company does not change what a person carries internally -- their beliefs, thoughts, and habitual responses. She explains that experiences like praise, criticism, failure, and fear shape recurring reactions that eventually feel like fixed personality traits rather than choices, and that changing the external environment only creates the feeling of a fresh start rather than actually resolving the underlying pattern. Using the example of someone who leaves a job over feeling unfairly criticized only to find the same defensiveness resurfacing in a new role, she argues that awareness -- not complete resolution -- is the necessary starting point for change, since awareness creates a gap between a triggering moment and the automatic response, and in that gap sits choice. Wright is careful to note the goal isn't to discard everything from one's past, since some inherited traits, like healthy scepticism or hard-won judgment, remain genuinely useful; the task is to distinguish what still serves from what has quietly become an obstacle to growth.
points: Wright's central claim: a fresh start changes where you are or the company you keep, but it doesn't change what comes with you -- geography and new relationships don't erase carried mental patterns.
Illustrative case: someone who leaves a job over feeling singled out by criticism finds relief in a new role, only to have the same defensiveness resurface once feedback starts arriving again.
Her diagnostic questions for spotting a carried pattern: What keeps happening and how do I usually respond? Where did I learn to respond this way? Does this response still serve me now?
Awareness, not full resolution, is presented as the necessary starting point: it creates a small gap between what happens and what you do next, and in that gap sits choice.
Not every inherited pattern needs to be discarded -- some, like healthy scepticism, remain useful; the task is distinguishing what still serves from what has become an obstacle.
quotes: A fresh start changes where you are or the company you keep, but it doesn't change what comes with you.

Growth and recovery are built on the understanding that unless we deliberately unpack and understand the beliefs, thoughts, and responses that we carry, they remain with us and will travel wherever we go.
Take someone who struggles with criticism at work. They feel singled out, believe feedback is unfair, and eventually leave because the workplace feels like the problem.
Then feedback arrives, and the same discomfort returns. Comments again feel personal, and the person again becomes defensive or starts questioning whether they are being treated fairly.
With awareness, you create a small gap between what happens and what you do next, and in that gap sits choice, the choice to grow.
Every construct we carry has history, but they don't all deserve a future. Several of mine felt like fixed parts of my personality for years.

Knowing what you carry doesn't mean living in the past. On the contrary, you only need to look back enough to understand what keeps turning up today, then turn your attention towards what you want to do next.
